## Problem 1

Please identify each of the following statements as true or false.
Each problem is worth one point.

### Part (a)

We usually consider parameters to be random.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

:::

### Part (b)

We usually consider parameters to be unknown.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True.

:::

### Part (c)

A statistic is a function of the population.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

:::

### Part (d)

A population can be infinite.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True.

:::

### Part (e)

We use the sample to draw conclusions about the population.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True.

:::

### Part (f)

If you know the expected value of $X$, you should be able to compute the
probability that $X$ is in any given range.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

:::

### Part (g)

The expected value is a measure of the spread of a distribution.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

:::

### Part (h)

The support of a random variable must be between 0 and 1.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

:::

### Part (i)

A statistic can have a distribution.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True.

:::

### Part (j)

"Statistic" is another word for "parameter."

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-dist
#| fig-cap: "Three distributions."
curve(expr = dnorm,
      from = -3,
      to = 6,
      ylab = "f(x)")
lambda <- function(x){
  dexp(x = x,
       rate = dnorm(0))
}
curve(expr = lambda,
      add = TRUE,
      lty = "aa")
lambda <- function(x){
  dgamma(x = x,
         shape = 2,
         rate = 0.6)
}
curve(expr = lambda,
      add = TRUE,
      lty = 3)
legend(x = "topright",
       legend = c("A",
                  "B",
                  "C"),
       lty = c("solid",
               "aa",
               "dotted"))
```

## Problem 2

(1 point)
Which of the distributions in @fig-dist
could describe the time in months
from diagnosis to death from a fatal form of cancer?
Select all that apply.

(a) A
(b) B
(c) C
(d) None of the above


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

B and C

:::

## Problem 3

(1 point)
In one to three sentences,
justify your answer to Problem 2.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}


The time to an event must be non-negative.
The support of distribution A includes negative values,
so it cannot be the distribution of the time to death.
The supports of distributions B and C are both non-negative,
so each could be the distribution of time to death.

Some students pointed out that diagnosis could be made via autopsy.
If a student said this in their justification and selected A, B, and C,
I gave them the points for both questions.

:::

## Problem 4

(1 point)
Which of the distributions in @fig-dist
is most likely to yield observations greater than 2?

(a) A
(b) B
(c) C
(d) It's impossible to tell from the information provided.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}


C

:::

## Problem 5

(1 point)
In one to three sentences,
justify your answer to Problem 4.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}


The height of distribution C is higher than the other distributions
for all values greater than 2.
Thus, the area under the curve to the right of 2 will be greatest for Distribution C.
Since area under the curve corresponds to probability,
Distribution C is most likely to yield observations greater than 2.

Some students described Distributions B and C as left-skewed,
which is incorrect. Both of these distributions are right-skewed.
The direction (left or right) refers to where the tail is, 
not where the hump is.

:::

## Problem 6

(1 point)
Identify the correct ordering of the expected values
of the distributions in @fig-dist,
from smallest to largest.

(a) A, B, C
(b) A, C, B
(c) B, A, C
(d) B, C, A
(e) C, A, B
(f) C, B, A

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

A, B, C

Distribution A is symmetric around zero, so its expected value is zero
(assuming the expected value exists).
Distributions B and C both have positive supports, so they must have positive expected values.
Because Distribution B has most of its mass close to zero
and Distribution C has most of its mass greater than zero,
the expected value of Distribution B should be less than the expected value of Distribution C.


:::


## Problem 7

(1 point)
Which of the distributions in @fig-dist
could describe the height in meters
of patients at primary care clinic?
Select all that apply.

(a) A
(b) B
(c) C
(d) None of the above


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

D

Nobody has a height less than zero and no one is more than four meters tall.

:::
